chunks: From him, from his father, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammad, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from some of his companions: Regarding a man who has money due from another man, and the debtor denies it and swears an oath of patience (yamin sabr), is there anything due to him?
He (peace be upon him) said: 'He is not permitted to demand it from him, and likewise if he considers it due at the hands of God, he is not permitted to demand it from him.'

key_terms.فِي ٱلرَّجُلِ: Regarding the man; a common opening for legal inquiries in hadith.
key_terms.يَجْحَدُهُ: He denies it; refers to the debtor's denial of the debt when asked.
key_terms.يَمِينَ صَبْرٍ: Oath of patience; an oath taken by a debtor to delay payment or deny a debt, after which the creditor cannot immediately force payment.
key_terms.ٱحْتَسَبَهُ: He considers it due; implies retaining the right to the debt as a divine claim or future right.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling of yamin sabr in Shia jurisprudence regarding debt disputes?
ai.summary: In the jurisprudence of *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith clarifies that the 'oath of patience' (*yamin sabr*) serves as a procedural bar to further litigation rather than extinguishing the debt itself. This ruling reflects the Shia scholarly view that the debtor’s oath resolves the immediate dispute in court, yet the creditor retains the right to pursue the debt later if new evidence emerges or if the debtor’s financial status changes, emphasizing the enduring validity of the obligation before God.
